name: Thirumagaraleeswarar Temple, Thirumagaral
deity: Shiva as Thirumagaraleeswarar (Magaraleeswarar), a self-manifested lingam shaped like a monitor lizard's tail, with the Goddess Thiribhuvana Nayaki
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, sung in the Tevaram by Sambandar (7th century); Chola origins, rebuilt in the Vijayanagara–Nayak period
dynasty: Chola, with Vijayanagara and Nayak rebuilding
summary: On the north bank of the Cheyyar south of Kanchipuram, the Lord of Thirumagaral is a self-manifested lingam shaped like a monitor lizard's tail — the form, tradition says, in which Shiva revealed himself to a Chola king.

sections.history: Thirumagaral is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and a Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu. Thirugnana Sambandar sang its Lord in a pathigam of eleven verses, which places the shrine among the sacred sites of the seventh century. The village lies on the northern bank of the Cheyyar river in Kanchipuram district, some 12 km north of Uthiramerur. Tradition holds that the first temple here was raised by the Cholas, and the king Rajendra is remembered in its legend; the masonry that stands today is largely of the Vijayanagara and Nayak period, around the sixteenth century. Local tradition also links the village's name to Makaran, an asura said to have been slain here.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east and is entered through a five-tiered rajagopuram. In the sanctum the self-manifested lingam of Thirumagaraleeswarar has an unusual form, likened to the tail of an udumbu, the monitor lizard, and the goddess Thiribhuvana Nayaki has her own shrine facing south. The temple tank is the Agni Theertham, and the sacred tree of the shrine is the lime.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that Shiva revealed himself to the Chola king Rajendra at this place in the very shape the lingam bears, the form of a monitor lizard's tail, and the king honoured the spot with a temple. Devotees see in the unusual lingam a sign that the Lord meets each seeker in his own way. The village name is also tied by tradition to the slaying of the asura Makaran.
sections.festivals: Pradosham, Maha Shivaratri and Karthigai Deepam are kept with special worship, together with the Arudra Darshan of Margazhi and the festivals of Thiribhuvana Nayaki. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Thirumagaral is a river-bank village shrine, peaceful and little visited, its gopuram rising above the fields along the Cheyyar. Pilgrims come to see the lizard-tail lingam and to sing Sambandar's verses before it. It combines well with the temples and Chola inscriptions of Uthiramerur to the south and with the shrines of Kanchipuram to the north.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples of the region. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Thirumagaral lies on the north bank of the Cheyyar, about 12 km north of Uthiramerur and roughly 20 km south of Kanchipuram by road. Kanchipuram and Chengalpattu are the nearest railway stations; Chennai International Airport, about 70 km away, is the nearest airport.
